results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** Nonzero complex Hilbert spaces $H,K$; vectors $u,u'\in H$, $v,v'\in K$; a trace-class $T$ on $H\widehat\otimes K$ with a nuclear representation $T=\sum_jT_{w_j,z_j}$, $w_j,z_j\in H\widehat\otimes K$; a bounded $A\in\mathcal B(H)$.

[F1] $T_{x,z}$ is trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) with $\|T_{x,z}\|_1=\|x\|\,\|z\|$, $\operatorname{tr}(T_{x,z})=\langle x,z\rangle$, and $T_{x,z}B=T_{x,B^*z}$, $BT_{x,z}=T_{Bx,z}$ for bounded $B$; for trace-class $T$, $\operatorname{tr}(TB)=\operatorname{tr}(BT)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle w_j,z_j\rangle$ for every nuclear representation ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-nuclear-bounded-cyclicity]], [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

[F2] $T$ is trace class exactly when $T=\sum_jT_{w_j,z_j}$ with $\sum_j\|w_j\|\,\|z_j\|<\infty$ converging in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]), and then $\|T\|_1=\inf\sum_j\|w_j\|\,\|z_j\|$; $\mathcal S_1$ is complete in trace norm and a two-sided ideal with $\|BTB'\|_1\le\|B\|\,\|T\|_1\|B'\|$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]).

[F3] If $S\in\mathcal S_1(H)$ and $x,y\in H$ then $\operatorname{tr}(ST_{x,y})=\langle Sx,y\rangle$; if $\operatorname{tr}(SA)=0$ for all bounded $A$ then $S=0$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-nuclear-bounded-cyclicity]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

[F4] Algebraic tensors are dense in the completed product, with the orthogonal coordinate norm formula; a closed span of a given countable sequence has a finite/countable orthonormal basis by Gram–Schmidt. Bounded tensor maps extend and satisfy the adjoint and norm identities; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds scalar coefficient sums ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]).



1.1 [The rank-one values] For $T_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}$ and bounded $A$, $T(A\otimes I)=T_{u\otimes v,(A\otimes I)^*(u'\otimes v')}=T_{u\otimes v,A^*u'\otimes v'}$ by [F1], whose trace is $\langle u\otimes v,A^*u'\otimes v'\rangle=\langle u,A^*u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle=\langle Au,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle$. On the other hand $\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\langle v,v'\rangle T_{u,u'})A\bigr)=\langle v,v'\rangle\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,u'}A)=\langle v,v'\rangle\langle Au,u'\rangle$ by [F1]. Hence the assignment $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}:=\langle v,v'\rangle T_{u,u'}$ satisfies the defining identity on rank-one tensors, and $\|\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}\|_1\le\|v\|\,\|v'\|\,\|u\|\,\|u'\|=\|u\otimes v\|\,\|u'\otimes v'\|$ by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 [Arbitrary rank-one vectors] Fix $w,z\in H\widehat\otimes K$. By density and Countable Choice choose sequences of finite algebraic tensors converging to these two vectors; collect their countably many second-factor vectors and let $K_0$ be their closed linear span. Finite rational complex combinations form an explicit dense sequence in $K_0$, so [F4] provides a finite/countable orthonormal basis $(f_b)$ of $K_0$. The maps taking $\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i$ to $\sum_i\langle v_i,f_b\rangle u_i$ have norm at most one by orthogonal coordinates and extend to the completion. Their values $w_b,z_b\in H$ satisfy $w=\sum_bw_b\otimes f_b$, $z=\sum_bz_b\otimes f_b$ and $\sum_b\|w_b\|^2=\|w\|^2$, $\sum_b\|z_b\|^2=\|z\|^2$: the finite-coordinate projections are contractions, converge on algebraic tensors in $H\odot K_0$, and hence converge on its closure, which contains $w,z$. Define $Q(w,z):=\sum_bT_{w_b,z_b}$. By [F1], [F2] and Cauchy–Schwarz, this converges in trace norm and $\|Q(w,z)\|_1\le\sum_b\|w_b\|\|z_b\|\le\|w\|\|z\|$. Finite-coordinate truncations and step 1.1 give $\operatorname{tr}(Q(w,z)A)=\langle(A\otimes I)w,z\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(T_{w,z}(A\otimes I))$; rank-one trace-norm continuity and bounded tensor maps [F4] pass this identity to limits. The identity uniquely determines $Q(w,z)$ by [F3], so it is independent of the supports, basis and approximants, is sesquilinear in $w,z$, and agrees with the elementary assignment. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, choose, construct, algebra]

3.1 [Extension to trace class] For a nuclear representation $T=\sum_jT_{w_j,z_j}$, define $\operatorname{Tr}_KT:=\sum_jQ(w_j,z_j)$. Step 2.1 and [F2] give trace-norm convergence and the bound $\|\operatorname{Tr}_KT\|_1\le\inf\sum_j\|w_j\|\|z_j\|=\|T\|_1$. The defining trace pairing follows by summing that of step 2.1, using trace-norm continuity and $\|A\otimes I\|\le\|A\|$. If two nuclear representations are used, both images have the same pairings against every bounded $A$, and their difference vanishes by [F3]. Thus the definition is independent of representation. The same uniqueness proves linearity, since the sum and scalar multiple of images satisfy the pairing for the sum and scalar multiple of inputs. This proves (a) and the elementary formula (c). [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 [Positivity and trace preservation] Step 2.1 gives $Q(w,w)=\sum_bT_{w_b,w_b}\ge0$, since $\langle T_{w_b,w_b}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,w_b\rangle|^2\ge0$ and trace-norm convergence implies operator-norm convergence. Every positive trace-class input has a positive spectral rank-one expansion by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]; the same proof applies when its trace is not one, by scaling when nonzero, and the zero input is immediate. The bounded map of step 3.1 carries its partial sums to positive sums of these $Q(w,w)$ and thus carries its limit to a positive operator. Taking $A=I_H$ in the defining pairing gives $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_KT=\operatorname{tr}T$. Hence density operators map to density operators. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra]

5.1 [Uniqueness] If two linear maps $\operatorname{Tr}_K,\operatorname{Tr}_K'$ satisfy the defining identity for all $T$ and $A$, then for fixed $T$ the difference $S=\operatorname{Tr}_KT-\operatorname{Tr}_K'T$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(SA)=0$ for all bounded $A$, so $S=0$ by [F3]. Hence the map is unique and, in particular, independent of any basis; the symmetrically defined $\operatorname{Tr}_H$ has the stated identity. [step 3.1, F3] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice, arbitrary nonzero complex Hilbert spaces $H,K$, and $\Psi\in H\widehat\otimes K$. The supports, bases and coefficient map are constructed in the proof; no countable basis of the ambient spaces is assumed.

[F1] Algebraic tensors are dense in their Hilbert completion, and orthogonal coordinates have the squared-norm sum formula. A given dense sequence in a Hilbert space yields a finite/countable orthonormal basis by Gram–Schmidt ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]).

[F2] Bounded finite-rank operators are compact, and an operator-norm limit of compact operators into a Hilbert space is compact under Countable Choice. Hilbert adjoints satisfy the adjoint identity and $(C^*)^*=C$; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds coordinate sums ([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]], [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]).

[F3] A compact positive self-adjoint operator has positive eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, accumulating only at zero, and its nonzero eigenspaces span the orthogonal complement of its kernel. A positive trace-class operator has trace and trace norm equal to the sum of its positive eigenvalues ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]], [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]]).

[F4] Rank-one operators have trace norm $\|T_{u,v}\|_1=\|u\|\|v\|$ and trace $\langle u,v\rangle$. The partial trace is bounded in trace norm with the defining bounded-operator pairing and elementary rank-one formula. Bounded tensor maps extend with their norm and adjoint identities ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-separable-partial-trace]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]).



1.1 [Countable supports and coefficients] By density and Countable Choice choose algebraic tensors $\Psi_n\to\Psi$ with finite factor decompositions. Their countably many factor vectors span closed subspaces $H_0,K_0$ with explicit dense sequences of finite rational complex combinations; [F1] supplies finite/countable orthonormal bases. The inclusion of $H_0\odot K_0$ in $H\widehat\otimes K$ is isometric and extends to its closed completion, which contains $\Psi$. Choose the basis $(f_j)$ of $K_0$. As in the orthogonal contraction construction of [[lem-nrqm-composites-separable-partial-trace]], coefficient contractions define $h_j\in H_0$ with $\Psi=\sum_jh_j\otimes f_j$ and $\sum_j\|h_j\|^2=\|\Psi\|^2$. All sums here may be finite or empty, including $\Psi=0$. [given, F1, F4, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 [The typed compact coefficient operator] Define $C(\sum_jz_j\bar f_j):=\sum_jz_jh_j$ first on finite sums in $\overline{K_0}$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|Cz\|\le(\sum_j\|h_j\|^2)^{1/2}\|z\|$, so it extends to all of $\overline{K_0}$ by continuity and completeness. The finite truncations $C_N$ have finite rank and $\|C-C_N\|\le(\sum_{j>N}\|h_j\|^2)^{1/2}\to0$, so [F2] makes $C$ compact. The adjoint has the correctly typed formula $C^*x=\sum_j\langle x,h_j\rangle\bar f_j$ for $x\in H_0$, hence $CC^*x=\sum_j\langle x,h_j\rangle h_j$. The finite sums $\sum_{j\le N}T_{h_j,h_j}$ converge in trace norm by [F4], with trace sum $\sum_j\|h_j\|^2$; their operator-norm limit is $CC^*$, so $CC^*$ is positive trace class with $\operatorname{tr}CC^*=\|\Psi\|^2$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, construct, algebra]

3.1 [Reduced-state identity] Let $\Psi_N=\sum_{j\le N}h_j\otimes f_j$. The elementary partial-trace formula gives $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{\Psi_N,\Psi_N}=\sum_{j\le N}T_{h_j,h_j}$, regarding the latter operators on $H$ as zero on $H_0^\perp$. Rank-one continuity and boundedness of the partial trace [F4] pass to the limit and give $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ extended by zero. Thus the nonzero eigenvalues of $CC^*$ are intrinsic to $\Psi$, independent of all auxiliary supports and bases. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, algebra]

4.1 [Singular vectors in the conjugate factor] By [F3] choose orthonormal eigenvectors $v_r\in H_0$ for the positive eigenvalues $s_r^2$ of $CC^*$, counted with multiplicity; finite-dimensional eigenspace bases are supplied by [F1] and their countable selection uses the stated Countable Choice. Define $\bar u_r:=s_r^{-1}C^*v_r\in\overline{K_0}$. Then $\langle\bar u_r,\bar u_t\rangle=s_r^{-1}s_t^{-1}\langle v_r,CC^*v_t\rangle=\delta_{rt}$, so the actual vectors $u_r\in K_0$ are orthonormal too. By step 2.1 their coefficients obey $u_r=\sum_js_r^{-1}\langle h_j,v_r\rangle f_j$. The trace formula [F3] gives $\sum_rs_r^2=\operatorname{tr}CC^*=\|\Psi\|^2$, and infinitely many positive eigenvalues tend to zero. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, choose, construct, algebra]

5.1 [Reconstruction] If $g\in\ker CC^*$ then $0=\langle CC^*g,g\rangle=\|C^*g\|^2$, so all $\langle g,h_j\rangle$ vanish. Thus every $h_j$ is in the closed span of the $v_r$ by [F3], and $h_j=\sum_r\langle h_j,v_r\rangle v_r$. The orthonormal series $\sum_rs_rv_r\otimes u_r$ converges in tensor norm because $\sum_rs_r^2<\infty$. Its $f_j$ coefficient is $\sum_rs_r\langle u_r,f_j\rangle v_r=\sum_r\langle h_j,v_r\rangle v_r=h_j$ by step 4.1. The orthogonal coefficient norm formula [F1] therefore identifies its sum with $\Psi$. If $\Psi=0$, the positive spectrum and the Schmidt family are empty, giving the zero expansion. [step 1.1, step 4.1, F1, F3, algebra]

6.1 [Purity and product criterion] For $\|\Psi\|=1$, steps 3.1–3.1 show that the reduced density has eigenvalues $s_r^2$ and $\sum_rs_r^2=1$, hence $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$. The difference $(\sum_rs_r^2)^2-\sum_rs_r^4=2\sum_{r<t}s_r^2s_t^2$ vanishes exactly when there is one positive coefficient. That case makes the expansion a product vector. Conversely for a nonzero product $a\otimes b$, its coefficients are $h_j=\langle b,f_j\rangle a$, so $C$ has rank one and $CC^*$ has one positive eigenvalue; for a unit product its reduced purity is one. All ambient Hilbert spaces remain arbitrary; only the supports of this particular vector were made countable. This establishes every claimed clause. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, $H$, $(M_r)$ with the normalization identity; a positive trace-class $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$.

[F1] $\|(M_r(x)\psi)_r\|_{\ell^2(H)}^2=\sum_r\|M_r(x)\psi\|^2$; the normalization hypothesis says the Bochner square norm is $\|\psi\|^2$, so the resulting equivalence class belongs to $L^2$ and has norm $\|\psi\|$ ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]).

[F2] For $T\in\mathcal S_1(H)$ the rank-one map $v\mapsto T_{v,v}$ is trace-norm continuous with $\|T_{v,v}\|_1=\|v\|^2$; $T_{x,z}B=T_{x,B^*z}$ and $\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\|B\|$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-nuclear-bounded-cyclicity]]).

[F3] A strongly measurable Banach-valued function is Bochner integrable exactly when the integral of its norm is finite; the Bochner integral is norm-continuous and dominated convergence holds under an integrable majorant ([[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]], [[lem-bochner-integral-norm-inequality]], [[thm-bochner-dominated-convergence]]).

[F4] Tonelli's theorem permits interchanging the nonnegative sum over $r$ and the integral over $X$; the trace pairing satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(T_{x,z})=\langle x,z\rangle$ and the polarisation/positivity properties of the previous items ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-separable-partial-trace]]).

[F5] Nuclear representations converge in trace norm as well as operator norm; finite rank-one sums are trace-norm dense, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v}A)=\langle Au,v\rangle$ for bounded $A$. Cauchy–Schwarz applies both to the countable coordinate sum and to the scalar integral ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]).

[F6] Monotone convergence applies to nonnegative scalar functions; scalar $L^2$ Cauchy–Schwarz and Minkowski give the integral product and sum bounds. Equality almost everywhere means equality outside a measurable null set ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).



1.1 [Construction and completeness of the Hilbert target] Coordinate Cauchy–Schwarz makes the inner product of $E=\ell^2(H)$ absolutely convergent and gives its squared norm $\sum_r\|z_r\|^2$. If $(z^{(n)})$ is Cauchy in this norm, each coordinate converges in the complete space $H$ to $z_r$; taking limits of finite squared sums shows $\sum_r\|z_r\|^2<\infty$ and $\|z^{(n)}-z\|_E\to0$. Thus $E$ is Hilbert. Strongly measurable $E$-valued fields have measurable norm and inner-product functions by their simple approximants; scalar Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] gives absolute integrability of the target inner product. This integral descends to the almost-everywhere quotient, is positive definite there, and has the stated norm; scalar Minkowski gives its triangle inequality. For completeness, take a Cauchy sequence of classes and a subsequence with representatives $f_k$ satisfying $\|f_{k+1}-f_k\|_2\le2^{-k}$; Countable Choice permits the countable representative selection. Set $d_k=f_{k+1}-f_k$. For $g_N:=\sum_{k\le N}\|d_k(\cdot)\|_E$, scalar Minkowski gives $\|g_N\|_2\le\sum_{k\le N}2^{-k}\le1$. Monotone convergence [F6] applied to $g_N^2$ gives $g:=\sum_k\|d_k\|_E\in L^2$ and $g<\infty$ almost everywhere. Hence $f_1+\sum_kd_k$ converges pointwise off a measurable null set in complete $E$; define its limit as zero on that set. The limit is strongly measurable: the countably many simple approximant ranges for all $f_k$ have a separable closed span, norm distances to a countable dense subset are measurable, and choosing the nearest of the first $N$ dense points gives finite-valued simple approximants converging pointwise. Scalar Minkowski and monotone convergence also give $\|f-f_k\|_2\le\sum_{j\ge k}2^{-j}\to0$, and $f\in L^2$ since $\|f\|_E\le\|f_1\|_E+g$. The original Cauchy sequence converges to the same class by the triangle inequality. Therefore the defined target is a Hilbert space; the construction uses no assumption that $\mu(X)$ is finite. [given, F1, F3, F6, choose, construct, algebra]

1.2 [Integrable cross fields] For $u,v\in H$, each $x\mapsto T_{M_r(x)u,M_r(x)v}$ is strongly measurable in trace norm by [F2]. By Cauchy–Schwarz twice and normalization,

2.1 [The $L^2$ isometry] Fix $\psi\in H$. The measurable nonnegative function $g_\psi(x):=\sum_r\|M_r(x)\psi\|^2$ has finite integral $\|\psi\|^2$, so it is finite outside a null set. On that set the finite coordinate truncations converge in $\ell^2(H)$; define the vector field to be zero on the exceptional null set. The truncations are strongly measurable and their pointwise limit is strongly measurable, as follows directly by approximation with simple functions (or by separability of $\ell^2(H)$ and measurable coordinates). The field belongs to $L^2(X;\ell^2(H))$ because its squared norm is $g_\psi$ almost everywhere. Its equivalence class defines $W\psi$, independently of the null-set representative. For any finite collection of vectors, the coordinate linear identities hold outside the union of their exceptional sets, so $W$ is linear as a map of equivalence classes; normalization gives $\|W\psi\|=\|\psi\|$, hence $W$ is a linear isometry. No $L^1$ integrability of this raw vector field is needed. [step 1.1, given, F1, F3, F6, construct, algebra]

3.1 [The PVM and the effects] Multiplication by $\mathbf1_B$ on $L^2$ is a bounded self-adjoint projection, with $P(X)=I$ and $P(B\cap C)=P(B)P(C)$. For disjoint $B_j$ with union $B$, the squared $L^2$ norm of $(P(B)-\sum_{j\le N}P(B_j))f$ is the integral of $\|f(x)\|^2$ over the tail of that disjoint union, and tends to zero by scalar dominated convergence. Thus $P$ is a PVM. Compression gives positive contractions $F(B)=W^*P(B)W$, normalization $F(X)=I$, and weak countable additivity. Equivalently, for every $u,v$, $\langle F(B)u,v\rangle=\int_B\sum_r\langle M_r(x)u,M_r(x)v\rangle\,d\mu$, with absolute convergence by Cauchy–Schwarz and normalization. This is the normalized POVM asserted in (b). [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]
$$\int_X\sum_r\|M_r(x)u\|\,\|M_r(x)v\|\,d\mu\le\|u\|\,\|v\|.$$
Thus, outside a null set, the rank-one series converges absolutely in trace norm. Its sum $K_{u,v}(x)$ is strongly measurable and Bochner integrable by [F3], with integrated norm at most $\|u\|\|v\|$. Define $E_B(u,v):=\int_BK_{u,v}(x)\,d\mu$. This is sesquilinear, satisfies $\|E_B(u,v)\|_1\le\|u\|\|v\|$, and has pairing $\operatorname{tr}(E_B(u,v)A)=\sum_r\int_B\langle A M_r(x)u,M_r(x)v\rangle d\mu$ for bounded $A$, by the boundedness of trace pairings and absolute integrability. In particular $E_B(u,u)$ is positive and $\operatorname{tr}E_B(u,u)=\langle F(B)u,u\rangle$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra]

4.1 [The bounded linear instrument] For a nuclear representation $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$, define $I_B(T):=\sum_jE_B(u_j,v_j)$, converging in trace norm. The bound of step 1.2 gives $\|I_B(T)\|_1\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. This is independent of representation: for a nuclear representation of zero, Tonelli and step 1.2 allow exchanging its $j$ sum, the $r$ sum and each bounded-$A$ trace pairing with the integral. For each fixed $r,x$, the two-sided ideal bound makes $\sum_jM_r(x)T_{u_j,v_j}M_r(x)^*=M_r(x)0M_r(x)^*=0$ in trace norm. Therefore all the resulting pairings vanish; rank-one test operators and [F5] show the image is zero. The difference of two representations is such a zero representation, proving independence. Hence $I_B$ is linear, bounded with norm at most one by taking the nuclear infimum, and positive by positive spectral rank-one expansion. For positive $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ its definition is exactly the Bochner formula in (c), and absolute integrability gives the stated bounded-$A$ pairing. Taking $A=I$ gives $\operatorname{tr}I_B(T)=\operatorname{tr}(TF(B))$ first for rank-one inputs by step 3.1 and then for all inputs by nuclear continuity; in particular $I_X$ is trace preserving. [step 3.1, step 1.2, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra]

5.1 [Countable additivity and complete positivity] For disjoint $B_j$ with union $B$, Bochner integrability gives $E_B(u,v)=\sum_jE_{B_j}(u,v)$ in trace norm. For a nuclear input, the sum of the norms of the omitted event tails is dominated term by term by $\|u_k\|\|v_k\|$; scalar dominated convergence passes countable additivity to $I_B(T)$ in trace norm. For each finite ancilla $\mathbb C^n$, act on $\mathbb C^n\widehat\otimes H$ with the pointwise Kraus maps $I\otimes M_r(x)$. For a vector $\xi=\sum_{k=1}^ne_k\otimes\xi_k$, the integrated squared output norm is $\sum_k\int_X\sum_r\|M_r(x)\xi_k\|^2d\mu=\|\xi\|^2$. The same construction as steps 1.2–3.1 therefore maps each positive rank-one $T_{\xi,\xi}$ to an integral of positive rank-one operators and extends positively to every positive trace-class amplified input. Expanding its finite ancilla matrix entries shows this extension equals the finite amplification of $I_B$. Thus every $I_B$ is completely positive, and together with additivity and trace preservation this establishes the full abstract instrument, not merely its restriction to positive inputs. [step 1.2, step 4.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

6.1 [Conditional updates] For a density operator $\rho$, $I_B(\rho)\ge0$ and $p(B)=\operatorname{tr}I_B(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F(B))$ by step 4.1. If $p(B)>0$, division gives a positive operator of trace one and hence the claimed density operator; if $p(B)=0$ no normalized update is defined. Nothing here claims a normalized singleton density or a universal representation theorem. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F2, algebra] ∎
